title: Parameters & Arguments
summary: Pass input values into methods: distinguish formal parameters in declarations from actual arguments in callers.
learningOutcomes: Match argument types, order, and count correctly
Understand automatic widening conversions during method calls

activities.title: Core Mechanics: Parameters & Arguments

breakdown.whatIsIt: Comprehensive exploration of Parameters & Arguments in Java.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Crucial for writing maintainable, reusable, and bug-free Java applications.
howItWorks: Decomposes complex logic into self-contained subprograms.
Allocates local variables on Call Stack frames.
Passes arguments by value, copying parameter data into frames.
Returns execution control back to caller upon reaching return statement.
keyTakeaways: Mastering Parameters & Arguments is essential for Java placement interviews and clean architecture.
Methods enforce the DRY principle by eliminating redundant duplicate code.
Parameters act as local placeholders; arguments provide runtime values.
Always consider edge cases such as invalid input parameters or stack overflow.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Parameters & Arguments
activities.description: Observe how argument values are evaluated and assigned positionally to formal parameters.

questions.prompt: What is the technical difference between a parameter and an argument?
options: Parameters are in the method declaration; arguments are the values passed at the method call
Arguments are in the method declaration; parameters are the values passed at the call
Parameters are numbers; arguments are Strings
There is no difference in any programming context
questions.explanation: Formal parameters are variables defined in the method declaration header; actual arguments are values/expressions supplied when the method is invoked.

questions.prompt: Given 'public static void compute(int a, double b)', which method call is valid?
options: compute(5.5, 10);
compute(10, 20);
compute(10);
questions.explanation: compute(10, 20) passes int 10 to int a, and int 20 is automatically widened to double 20.0 for double b. In option A, double 5.5 cannot fit into int a without explicit casting.

questions.prompt: What happens if you pass 3 arguments to a method that declares only 2 parameters?
options: The 3rd argument is ignored
A compile-time error occurs indicating no matching method signature was found
The 3rd argument is stored in a global variable
The method runs twice
questions.explanation: Java strictly enforces arity. Passing fewer or more arguments than declared produces a compile-time error.

questions.prompt: How does Java match arguments to parameters when multiple parameters are present?
options: Alphabetically by variable name
Strictly from left to right by position (index order)
By largest memory size first
Randomly based on CPU scheduling
questions.explanation: Arguments are matched to parameters positionally from left to right.

questions.prompt: Can you pass an arithmetic expression such as 'x * 2 + 5' as a method argument?
options: No, only raw literal numbers or single variable names are allowed
Yes, Java evaluates the expression first and passes the resulting value to the parameter
Only if the expression is enclosed in quotes
Only inside while loops
questions.explanation: Expressions are fully evaluated at runtime before the method is invoked, and the evaluated value is bound to the parameter.

questions.prompt: If method 'printAge(int age)' is called with 'printAge((int) 25.8)', will it compile?
options: No, casting inside argument lists is forbidden
Yes, the explicit cast truncates 25.8 to int 25, which matches parameter 'int age'
It compiles but throws an ArithmeticException
It prints 25.8
questions.explanation: Explicit casting (int) 25.8 narrows the double to integer 25, perfectly satisfying the int parameter.

questions.prompt: What is the scope of a formal parameter variable?
options: It is accessible anywhere in the entire project
It is local to the method body in which it is declared
It is accessible across all methods in the same class
It exists until the computer reboots
questions.explanation: Parameters are local variables whose scope is restricted strictly to the body of the method.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes passing arguments by name (named arguments like name="Alex") in Java?
options: Java supports named arguments using the colon operator
Java does NOT support named arguments; argument binding is strictly positional
Java supports named arguments if you import java.util.NamedArgs
Java supports named arguments in all static methods
questions.explanation: Unlike Python or Kotlin, Java does not support named argument syntax. Parameter binding is strictly positional.

practice.title: Personalized Greeting with Age
practice.problemStatement: Write a method named 'printProfile' that takes a String 'name' and an int 'age'. It prints: 'Name: <name> | Age: <age>'. In main(), call it with 'Liam' and 21.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between formal parameters and actual arguments?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Formal parameters are variables defined in the method signature declaration that receive values. Actual arguments are the concrete values, variables, or expressions passed into the method by the caller when the method is invoked.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Can actual argument names differ from formal parameter names?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes, absolutely. The parameter name exists only inside the method's local scope. The caller can pass any variable name, literal value, or expression. Matching is determined by position and type, never by identifier name.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Explain automatic widening conversion in method invocations.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: If a method expects a wider primitive type (such as double or long) and the caller passes a narrower compatible type (such as int or float), Java automatically widens the value without requiring explicit casting. However, narrowing conversions (e.g. double to int) require an explicit cast.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Does Java support default argument values like Python or C++ (e.g. void log(String msg, int level = 1))?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. Java does not support default parameter values. To achieve default arguments in Java, developers use method overloading—defining another method with fewer parameters that forwards calls to the fuller method with default values.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: In what order are method arguments evaluated when expressions are passed?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In Java, arguments are evaluated strictly from left to right before the method is entered. For example, in method(expr1, expr2), expr1 is fully evaluated before expr2 begins evaluation.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What is 'arity' in method design?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Arity refers to the number of arguments or parameters a method takes. A method with zero arguments is nullary, one argument is unary, two is binary, and multiple is n-ary. Clean code principles recommend keeping arity to 3 or fewer parameters whenever possible.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What is varargs in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Varargs (variable-length argument lists) allows a method to accept zero or more arguments of a specified type using the ellipsis syntax: 'void printAll(String... items)'. Internally, Java treats varargs as an array. It must always be the last parameter in the declaration.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

activities.title: Self-Mastery Checklist
checklist: Parameters: Variables declared in the method header (formal parameters).
Arguments: Concrete values or expressions supplied at the call site (actual arguments).
Positional Matching: Java binds arguments to parameters strictly left-to-right by position.
Automatic Widening: Narrower primitives (e.g., int) automatically widen to match wider parameter types (e.g., double).
No Default Arguments: Java achieves default parameters via method overloading, not default syntax.
